items.body: EMEFE spent nine years watching “Sun Spat” live a life they never planned for it. Written by saxophonist Jas Walton and tucked into the band’s 2015 self-titled album as a deep cut, it was never released as a single, and never backed by any promotional machinery. It just moved. Slowly, through streaming algorithms and word of mouth, the track gathered millions of plays, a quiet breakout for a New York horn-led ensemble that had already gone on indefinite hiatus in 2016. The live version captured here, “Sun Spat Live in Brooklyn,” was recorded at The Sultan Room in Bushwick and filmed by Isaac Gillespie. It appears on the band’s new four-track EP Sun Spat 2026, released 22 May. The performance features a nine-piece lineup: Walton on tenor sax, Lynn Ligammari on baritone sax, Julie Acosta on trumpet, Aani Kisslinger on trombone, Miles Francis on drums, Doug Berns on bass, Jake Pinto on keys, Harry Terrell and Tim Allen on guitars, and Javier Ramos on congas and percussion. Mixed and mastered by Shiftee, the Brooklyn-based mix engineer and two-time DMC World Champion, with live recording by Sharif Mekawy. EMEFE formed in 2009 when Francis, then a 19-year-old freshman at NYU who had just joined Antibalas and was studying under afrobeat pioneer Tony Allen, assembled a group of jazz school classmates drawn to Fela Kuti’s rhythmic architecture. Over time, the band folded in funk, new wave and neo-soul, keeping the horn section as the ensemble’s lead voice and Berns’s bass as its anchor. Members went on to tour with Mark Ronson, David Byrne, The Roots and Sharon Jones during the hiatus years, but “Sun Spat” kept pulling people in. When EMEFE reconvened for their 2025 album FORWARD and played sold-out rooms, Francis asked the crowd who was seeing the band for the first time. Most of the room put their hands up. But when the band played “Sun Spat,” every one of them already knew the words. Listen to and get your copy of Sun Spat 2026 following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: EMEFE – Sun Spat (Live in Brooklyn) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: EMEFE是一支来自纽约的九人乐队，以afrobeat为根基，融合放克、新浪潮和新灵魂乐元素，铜管乐组在编曲中担任主导声部。乐队成员大多出身爵士院校，受Fela Kuti节奏体系影响，鼓手Miles Francis早年在NYU师从afrobeat先驱Tony Allen并加入Antibalas。作品《Sun Spat》原收录于2015年同名专辑，经流媒体算法自然传播积累了数百万播放量。此次Brooklyn现场版由九人编制完成，录音混音由两届DMC世界冠军Shiftee操刀。整体音乐定位偏向非裔流派的当代演绎与世界节律的延续，编曲扎实但实验性与前卫性有限，更接近传统funk/afrobeat框架内的成熟融合表达。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The whole is not always greater than the sum of its parts... and Curved Air functioned differently depending on which members were in the band.The quartet, comprised of Darryl Way on violin, Francis Monkman on keyboards, piano, and electric guitar, Florian Pilkington-Miksa on drums, and Sonja Kristina on vocals, with occasional changes in bassist, would produce three essential albums that would cement the prestige, sound, and subsequent legacy of a band that, as its name suggests, took as many turns as the wind, guiding the violin strings and the vocal cords of one of the best singers in classic progressive rock, an ideal partner for the other leading lady of progressive rock, Annie Haslam, since they had distinct registers and styles, much like Janis Joplin and Grace Slick in psychedelic rock.It Happened Today already fully showcases the style, supported by that trident formed by Monkman's piano and guitar, Sonja's voice and Darrl Way's violin, which after a strong section at the beginning, almost like a plea thrown to the sky, helped to rise by the piano...receives its answer in the second part of the song, with the violin completing the scheme, showing what will be the classic Curved Air format...to which it is not advisable to get used to, because they will be systematically changing it throughout this debut album, as well as the initial trilogy.In Stretch it is evident that the path had not yet been fully found, and it is a psychedelic blues very much in the Jefferson Airplane range, both the singing and the instrumentation, which in any case is still very good, especially when the violin and guitar share the solo.In Screw they already began a style that they would later deepen...a very special treatment of the melody, where they take it out of tune, seem to go backwards, then move forward, with the violin right in front, and then go back again with the organ. Vivaldi will be their classic, with Darryl Way showcasing not only his skill but also his sensitivity, backed by Francis Monkman on guitar, adding a drama...a force, a passion, classic hard rock, so to speak, because Curved Air always sounded sophisticated and raw at the same time, unafraid to get their shoes dirty while rocking, as well as later venturing into more complex territory. The second part of Vivaldi is pure violin improvisation, joined by the guitar, leading into the grand finale.Hide And Seek is almost an experiment with Sonja singing almost lyrically, with the band playing a wild, distorted, psychedelic rock improvisation; the way her voice is combined with the instruments, and even the echo effect, speaks of the mature composition. With an ending that the piano takes in another direction, which gives it even more value, and solos that Black Sabbath could have used.Propositions will be yet another prime example of premature stylistic crystallization, with its accelerated, rock-infused opening, followed by the expansive array of guitar, bass, and violin, where at times Sonja can sing as wildly as Maggie Bell of Stone the Crowes. The violin interrupting the rock, like a knife slicing through canvas, will work its magic in the memory of every listener.Rob One is a respite ballad to enjoy that magic of the violin, with the piano and drums, again the chemistry of this quartet, even in an instrumental track without Sonja. Situations is the fourth track on the album, where the band is already present in all its splendor. It begins subtly, softly... with an almost theatrical stage presence from Sonja's performance, which she maintains throughout this period and which contributes to the sound of Curved Air.A melody reminiscent of doll boxes follows a more visceral one, albeit with a mellotron in the background, those theatrical faces that represent the spectrum of emotions from drama to pure joy... all represented on this debut album where the search had already begun, reaching at times those same stars they would later definitively claim.
items._cn_summary: Curved Air 1970年首张专辑将古典小提琴引入前卫摇滚框架，融合硬摇滚、迷幻布鲁斯与巴洛克元素。Sonja Kristina的人声与Darryl Way的小提琴形成核心对话，Francis Monkman的键盘与电吉他提供多变织体支撑。专辑展现早期前卫摇滚的实验精神，包含不协和旋律处理、自由即兴段落与非常规结构安排。Vivaldi一曲将巴洛克主题与硬摇滚力量结合，Hide and Seek则探索迷幻与即兴边界。作为英国前卫摇滚早期代表，作品在摇滚与古典之间搭建桥梁。Warner Bros厂牌发行，具有一定主流属性。整体创新性集中在小提琴主导的编制与古典元素的融合上，但未深入触及先锋实验、爵士即兴或电子声响等领域。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — While ITOIZ was one of the most popular acts to emerge from the prog rock boom from the Basquespeaking region of Spain in the late 70s, this band actually extended its career far beyond its 1974formation and made it all the way to 1988 before disbanding but like virtually every other Spanishprogger to play catch up during a small window of time that emerged after the collapse of the Francoregime and the end of the prog window closing at the end of the 1970s, ITOIZ too had to simplify itsmusic to join the world of radio friendly pop music although the band continued to performexclusively in the Basque language. Following its 1978 self-titled debut the band had one more progrelease in them with its second album EZEKIAL before succumbing to pressures of the marketplace.This sophomore release expanded the core five members to include a three additional musicians thatadded the violin, mandolin, saxophone, cuatro and extra piano. In addition to that an additionalvocalist and children's choir. This was the band's most acclaimed release.As the title suggests this is indeed a concept album referring to the prophet EZEKIAL which thealbum uses as a template for related biblical themes. The album followed the trend of Basque progacts eschewing the Andalusian flamenco influences and infusing the local folk flavors with elementsof progressive rock and jazz. The flute aspects evoked the fluttering tenderness of a classic JethroTull album while the dreamy pastoral folk passages seemed more inspired by Genesis or Camelespecially with the thick atmospheric keyboards adding layers of dreamy ambience however musicallythe melodic touches were fueled by Basque folk with the contrast emerging in more powerful guitarrock. The album features eight tracks with each tackling a different theme based on the prophet. Thealbum runs about 37 minutes and displayed a much more ambitious last hoorah for its prog leaningsbefore plummeting into the simplified pop arena devoid of any such complexities. The album is a lot mellower than even the mellow debut with its acoustic-fueled folk aspects as theunderpinning that finds the world of rock and jazz invited over to have a conversation. The opening'Ezekielen Prophezia' sets the stage with a standard introduction to the flavors of the debut alongwith the addition of a violin. As the tracks continue the saxophone is added and by the third trackwe find a strange mix of symphonic keyboards melding with a Tull-ish flute flurry and a smooth jazzsaxophone joining in which to my ears is the weakest part. Imagine if you will Kenny G joining Cameland Tull for a jam and you'd not be too far off. The album continues these same characteristics withvocalist Juan Carlos P'rez delivering the same somewhat underwhelming vocals that were present onthe debut. The fourth track simply titled 'Ezekiel' features the children's choir along with asimple campfire type of guitar accompaniment. It's a bit campy actually and sounds rather out ofplace. For my ears the first half of the album sounds rather clunky without any true cohesiveness to asupposedly concept album and the musical deliveries are very steeped in progressiveness. It's notreally until the fifth track 'Ezekielen Ikasgaia' where the albums comes to life with Itziar Egileorpicking up vocal duties which makes me wonder why she wasn't the lead vocalist on the whole album asshe blows the dude away big time however once again the Kenny G soft sax parts rub me the wrong wayespecially with the psychedelic organs by their side since it all seems to cancel each other for theproper effect. The best tracks for me are the ending ones. 'Ezekielen Ametsa' at last offers somemore interesting song structures and vocal performances (by the girl) which basically continues intothe following track 'Ezekielen Erantzuna.' Here the band sounds more in sync and the elements geltogether much better which is thankfully features less sax interruptions. Overall this is a decentalbum but too many irritating aspects for me to warm up to. So many other better Basque bands IMHOso i'm not sure why this one has appealed to so many more than the rest.
items._cn_summary: ITOIZ是来自西班牙巴斯克地区的渐进民谣乐队，《Ezekiel》是其第二张专辑，延续了巴斯克民间音乐与英国前卫摇滚融合的路线。专辑以圣经先知以西结为主题概念，邀请小提琴、曼陀林、萨克斯等乐手扩充编制，融入了民谣、前卫摇滚与爵士元素。评论中将其与Jethro Tull、Genesis、Camel等英国前卫摇滚代表相比，长笛与键盘营造出梦幻田园氛围，但萨克斯段落被批评为接近轻爵士，与前卫摇滚的气质不太协调。整体风格偏温和内敛，人声表现力有限。作为巴斯克语原创作品，具有一定的地域文化独特性，但整体仍属于传统渐进摇滚框架内的作品，实验性和创新性有限。

items.body: Post-punk icon Peter Murphy has released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” as a single via Metropolis Records. The track is a reworking of “Swoon,” the lead single from Murphy’s 2025 album “Silver Shade”. The original “Swoon” was issued in February 2025, featuring Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails on backing vocals and album producer Youth on bass. The new remix comes from the U.S. dream-pop duo Magic Wands (Dexy and Chris Valentine). “Our take on the song was about chasing a very specific feeling, like a kind of natural high,” the duo explain. “The goal was to build on the emotion in Peter’s vocal and surround it with a fast-moving, euphoric wash of guitars and synths, capturing the rush of a true swoon.” About Peter Murphy Peter Murphy is an English singer born in Northampton in 1957. He co-founded Bauhaus in 1978, and the band’s debut single, the nine-minute “Bela Lugosi’s Dead,” was released in 1979. Bauhaus recorded four studio albums before splitting in 1983, and the band has reformed several times since. Side-Line has reported on the group’s activity, including a 2018 world tour announcement alongside David J and the cancellation of a 2022 North American run. Peter Murphy’s solo career began in 1986 with “Should The World Fail To Fall Apart” (Beggars Banquet) and continued through “Love Hysteria” (1988), “Deep” (1989) — which included the U.S. single “Cuts You Up” — “Holy Smoke” (1992) and “Cascade” (1995). His later records reflected his interest in Sufism and his adopted home of Turkey, and the catalogue extends to “Lion” (2014), produced by Killing Joke bassist Youth. After a heart attack in 2019, which Side-Line reported as he announced his first live date back with Bauhaus, Murphy returned to recording. His studio album “Silver Shade,” billed as his tenth solo full-length and reuniting him with producer Youth, was released by Metropolis Records on May 9, 2025, as Side-Line reported at the time. The record features contributions from Trent Reznor, Tool’s Danny Carey and Justin Chancellor, and Boy George, who duets on the closing track “Let The Flowers Grow.” That song was later issued in remixes by Juno Reactor and Delerium. The album was preceded by the singles “Swoon” and “The Artroom Wonder.” Metropolis Records now issues “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix),” a reworking of the “Silver Shade” track, released on May 29, 2026.
items._cn_summary: 本文为Side-Line发布的新闻稿，报道后朋克传奇人物Peter Murphy（原Bauhaus主唱）单曲「Swoon」的Magic Wands混音版发行。原文以资讯形式梳理了Murphy的职业生涯与近期专辑「Silver Shade」的背景信息。该作品原版联合了Trent Reznor、Tool乐队成员及Boy George等跨领域音乐人，混音版本由美国梦幻流行二人组操刀，以吉他与合成器构建迷幻层次。在音乐取向上，该作品横跨后朋克、梦幻流行与哥特摇滚，与暗潮/后朋克审美有较高契合度，同时Trent Reznor与Tool成员的参与为原版带来工业与前卫摇滚的基因。然而本文为纯新闻性质，缺乏深度评论与艺术分析，且混音手法描述偏常规，整体信息量与原创性有限。

items.body:
It’s been a lengthy wait for the fourth album from Finnish accordionist Teija Niku, but she’s hardly been idle over the last few years. Between the pandemic, giving birth, and the death of her mother, her time has been filled. But the long pause makes this return all the sweeter, with its joyful exploration of the places where the music of her homeland intersect with her deep love of Balkan music.

That’s amply illustrated on her composition “Finsko Dajchovo,” inspired by the Bulgarian folk dance rhythm, a loving creation that moves sprightly and gracefully, or “Seitsemän,” taking its cue from Macedonian love songs. The bright, springlike melody, light, full of promise and hope could have been written for eager dancing feet.

Everywhere, Niku displays her acute sense of melody. “Elokuu,” a celebration of the late summer lights of August, is a lilting, wistful piece, yet tinged with shades of melancholy for the winter to come, a masterful evocation of shifting moods.

While the influence of Balkan music hovers over Tovi (the title, according to Niku, translates as “an undefined bit of time, somewhere between a moment and a while”), a Nordic sensibility remains very much at its heart, with a couple of soaring polskas to move things briskly along, in a contrast to the brief, shadowy, brooding opener “Ohto.”

But the real heart of the disc comes at the very end, with “Poloneesi äidille,” a piece Niku composed for her mother’s 70th birthday, three years before she died. It’s a soft, elegiac work that suddenly becomes transcendent as she begins to sing, You can hear that this performance is completely from the heart, and it is a beautiful way to finish. Now to hope that it’s not such a long gap before she’s back in the studio.

Find the artist online.

Further listening:

Duo Ruut - Ilmateade

Maria Moramarco, Fabio Mina, and Francesco Savoretti - Pietrafonie

Jaune Toujours - Vertigo

items._cn_summary: 芬兰手风琴演奏家Teija Niku的第四张专辑《Tovi》，将北欧芬兰民乐传统与巴尔干民间音乐进行跨界融合。专辑以手风琴为核心乐器，曲目灵感源自保加利亚民间舞蹈节奏与马其顿情歌，旋律明亮活泼，兼具北欧内敛深沉的抒情气质。末曲《Poloneesi äidille》为献给她已故母亲而作的挽歌，情感深沉真挚。整体属于原声民乐范畴内的跨文化融合，在世界音乐领域具有清晰的地域特色和跨界意识，但缺少实验性声响设计、电子元素或前卫手法，在创新性和制作层面相对传统。与用户偏好的实验、前卫、爵士、电子及暗潮方向重合度有限，仅在世界音乐类别中有一定对应。

items.body:
This collaboration between the five-piece Belgian instrumental group Wör, whose members specialize in bringing the music of earlier centuries to life, and Kongero, the acclaimed Swedish female acapella folk quartet, offers an unusual chance to explore how their two cultures, ostensibly so different, can come together. It might sounds an unlikely mix, but here’s a spoiler: it turns out they’re pretty much musical best friends.

The album kicks off at a cracking pace with “Var Är Du?”, a bravura performance through a twisted, tortuous piece that manages to be both elegant and surprising. However, the true astonishment arrives at the end, when the audience applauds and you suddenly realize this was recorded live (actually over two separate performances).

The musicians bring material from their separate traditions, plus one original, showcasing their skills in intricate, swinging arrangements for both instruments and voices. Thanks to their skill, the varied ideas fit together seamlessly so it’s brimming with delights, like the wonderfully-titled “Drinking Like A Sweet Swede,” where the singers layers their harmonies over a jaunty backing. Everything is intricate, performed with a glowing precision that can disarm the senses with its beauty.
The highlight, perhaps, is the beautiful “Klosterjungfrun.” The slow, seductive opening draws in the listener, the voices airy and light, curling around each other as the instruments wind long their path their. It’s a beautiful piece, but really, just one gem among so many here.

There’s never a foot wrong, no note out of place and the performances are passionate, stellar, a true collaboration of instruments and voices. Add to that a mix that’s sharp as a razor, and Songbooks Live is a truly outstanding album, a perfect illustration that people have more in common than separates them. And it illustrates exactly what artists can achieve live. With luck, they’ll work together again. Soon, please.

Find the artists online.

Kongero

WÖR

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — Was the wait worth it? A crucial question, given that DIFFERENT LIGHT's previous album dates back to 2020, six long years to discover the sequel to "Binary Suns - Part One," logically titled "Binary Suns - Part Two." Frankly, the answer is a resounding yes, as Trevor Tabone has crafted captivating and breathtakingly beautiful melodies. As a concept album, it's once again difficult to categorize the twenty tracks.It's worth noting that with the Progressive Gears label having ceased operations, DIFFERENT LIGHT has found a home with Shaded Moon Entertainment, a Dutch company dedicated to progressive and metal music.Four mini-suites form the core of the album. What are the strengths of this work? Undoubtedly, the melody in all its forms; Trevor Tabone is an absolute master of this genre. The gentleman sings very well, and even more so; on many occasions, I feel like I'm hearing the four Liverpool musicians in the vocal harmonies, or the Barclay James Harvest of their golden age when Woolly was still with the band, setting the stage for the underlying symphonic dimension ("The Singularity"). This symphonic quality is also present in the following track, "Labour of Love," enhanced by a superb six-string solo from Petr Lux.The show continues from the very start of the second suite, "The Syncretist," with the brilliant, energetic, and remarkably effective instrumental "Sober Dancing," which segues into "Pillage of Souls," in the same vein but with vocals and, again, very much in the Liverpool style.The track I like the least on the entire album is the one that was premiered: "A Fool's Errand." Not bad, but below the rest of the album in my opinion, more generic (which is what I felt after several listens), incredibly radio-friendly. "Constant Silver Lining," which then unfolds in four sections, features Petr Lux playing a virtuoso piece reminiscent of Ulrich Jon Roth. It's a very rock-oriented track compared to the rest of the album, illuminated by Trevor Tabone's magical piano playing, and concludes with a very successful polyphonic choral arrangement (ooh ooh... and ah ah...), one of my favorite passages on the entire "Binary Suns Part Two."We still have "Stalker Talks" in three parts, energetic in its introduction (with Petr Lux still front and center), followed by a piano/vocal passage of absolute finesse (reminiscent of vintage Barclay James Harvest's "Everyone is Everybody Else"), a rhythm section (Jiri Matousek and David Filak) at the peak of their powers, pure musical pleasure in a single, concise phrase.The closing track, "The Last Call," says it all in its title, too short for my liking, an enchanting melody where the four instrumentalists unite in a brilliant finale that makes you want to hit replay.Originally published on Profilprog.com
items._cn_summary: 《Binary Suns (Part 2)》是马耳他/捷克音乐人Trevor Tabone领衔的乐队Different Light于2026年推出的跨界前卫摇滚概念专辑，由荷兰独立厂牌Shaded Moon Entertainment发行。专辑共二十首曲目，结构上由四组迷你组曲构成，核心特征是旋律性强的人声和声与交响化编曲，评论中多次将其与披头士的声部编排及Barclay James Harvest的黄金时期相比较。吉他手Petr Lux的演奏受Ulrich Jon Roth影响，偏向摇滚化表达。整体定位偏向可听性较高的传统交响前卫路线，融合古典管弦乐色彩与摇滚器乐段落，概念性强但实验性有限。

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — The last dinosaur of progressive music, chapter twenty-three as far as studio albums are concerned. Their previous album, "Mirror to the Sky," released in May 2023, was a good record, despite what the many naysayers here, there, and elsewhere might say.Certainly, Yes will never recreate "Fragile," "Close to the Edge," or "Relayer" for many reasons, and good reasons at that. Times have changed, the musicians involved are no longer the same, with only Steve Howe remaining on guitar. Recording techniques are different too, and Roger Dean's signature style, now carried on by his children, remains for the visual aspect.Jon Davison had a lot of trouble taking over the vocal duties, Jon Anderson remaining irreplaceable, but this finally seems to have been resolved over the last two albums.Among the interesting features of this new album is the use of the Czech Symphony Orchestra on two occasions, which breathes new life into the classic Yessian music, as was already the case on "Magnification" in 2000. Interestingly, these two pieces are among the best: "Aurora" (9/10) and "Ariadne" (8/10). How to reproduce them on stage remains a mystery for now; we'll find out in 2027. Regarding the two bonus tracks, while "Watching the River Roll" is still listenable (6/10) as background music, the same cannot be said for "Jambustin" (4/10).Other highlights of "Aurora," in the order presented, include "Loves Lies Dreaming" (8/10), where Steve Howe shines on acoustic guitars; the epic "Countermovement" (9/10), which, while a bit slow to get going, has an excellent second half; and "Emotional Intelligence" (7/10), reminiscent of the delicate "Wonderous Stories" (which makes us feel old).As for the tracks not mentioned (2, 6, and 7), I'll let you judge for yourselves. Personally, I found "Aurora" significantly inferior to "Mirror to the Sky," which was very harshly criticized by many three years ago.Originally published on Profilprog.com
items._cn_summary: Yes乐队第二十三张录音室专辑《Aurora》，延续交响前卫摇滚路线，邀请捷克交响乐团参与两首曲目的录制，复刻2000年《Magnification》式的管弦配器策略。评论者肯定了开场曲《Aurora》及长篇曲目《Countermovement》的后半段表现，指出Steve Howe的古典吉他段落仍具亮点，同时也对部分曲目和两首附赠曲表示失望。整体评价认为该作明显逊于前作《Mirror to the Sky》。Yes作为老牌英式前卫摇滚代表，已不可能重现七十年代经典时期的实验性与锋芒，当前阵容仅余Steve Howe一位元老，制作趋于保守的交响化包装，面向怀旧听众群体，与追求前卫实验的音乐取向存在一定距离。

items.body: Review by Matti — -- The First Review --There is one rather frustrating downside to this compilation: the lack of release years of the source albums. That said, the listened surely would also appreciate some liner notes, too. At least the musicians with their intruments are listed trackwise, as well as composers, and the source albums albeit sadly without the years. Therefor especially for the timeline you are driving blind, so to speak, unless you do online search while listening. I won't be doing that now, so my review concentrates on the musical contents. And they are quite interesting! In general, it seems that most progheads only appreciate/remember Curved Air's early classic era featuring both violinist Darryl Way and keys/guitar player Francis Monkman, ie. the first three albums '70 -' 72. True, the band's later phases, built around vocalist Sonja Kristina, are uneven and a bit messy, but all the more positively this 2-disc set can surprise you. I guess nearly all material here dates from this Millennium, perhaps with some 90's thrown in. Four tracks come from the 2014 Curved Air album North Star which I have given a warm review. The next biggest representation of Curved Air itself is for Reborn (2008). The point of this set, however, is to represent also solo projects of Kristina, Way, Monkman and the numerous musicians who have contributed to the band's later eras. Just too bad there are no liner notes, because this is exactly such release where they would be very useful and valuable. The songs from Reborn actually sound pretty good in their modern production. 'Screw' was a new version of the song from the CA debut Air Conditioning. One track is (prev. unreleased) from the Reborn sessions and another is a Japanese only bonus track. Kristina, Way and the original CA drummer Florian Pilkington-Miksa were accompanied by guitarist Andy Christie.Of solo projects of Darryl Way is here represented Children Of The Cosmos and its fine title track. Monkman's solo harpsichord recording of H�ndel's Suite No. 7 (Ouverture) is among the numerous previously unreleased tracks, like also the Way & Kristina collaboration 'Ichiban Girl'.Bassist Mike Wedgwood sings his own laid-back, blues-flavoured song 'Coming Out'. 'Towards Tomorrow' is a fusiony instrumental from Curved Space which was practically a jam-based brainchild of Monkman and Pilkington-Miksa. 'Shame' is a bluesy vocal track from guitarist Kirby Gregory's solo album. Drummer Stewart Copeland (of The Police fame, and Sonja's husband) offers his previously unreleased piece performed with a symphony orchestra.CD 2 contains several more previously unreleased tracks, and quite nice ones, such as violinist Paul Sax's (and keyboardist Robert Norton's) instrumental 'By the Fire'. 'Moon Beams' is an ethereal, beautiful collaboration of Kristina and Norton, and 'One Step Forward' an elegant instrumental for three bass guitars, by Chris Harris. 'Labyrinth' is a 13-minute instrumental composed by Norton, Pilkington-Miksa and Gregory. Kit Morgan plays all instruments on his Eclectica Historica breezy instrumental piece 'The Gift', and so does drummer Andy Tween on his 'Paraselenae'. The set is closed by Curved Air's lovely Yes tribute 'Soon' where Kristina has rather Jon Anderson -like vocals.All in all, this is a very versatile and pleasant set, and a solid proof of the high level of musical talent that has graced Curved Air's later periods. With proper information and liner notes my 3,5 stars would definitely have been rounded up.
items._cn_summary: 这张双碟合辑收录了英国前卫摇滚乐队Curved Air后期阶段的录音及其成员的个人项目作品。核心内容来自2008年专辑《Reborn》和2014年《North Star》，并包含多首此前未发行的曲目。音乐风格横跨前卫摇滚、融合爵士、布鲁斯、古典管弦乐等方向，展现了乐队成员在小提琴、键盘、贝斯、鼓等不同乐器上的个人探索。其中Stewart Copeland的交响乐团配器作品、Chris Harris的三把贝斯器乐曲以及Francis Monkman的羽管键琴独奏展现了跨界融合的意图。整体而言，这是一张偏向传统前卫摇滚的家族汇编合辑，缺乏强烈的实验性或前卫探索，定位介于主流前卫摇滚与轻度跨界融合之间。

items.body: Review by James Lee — I'm in the minority here (not unusual) in that I greatly prefer Klaatu's first album. Having said that, there's no doubt in my mind that Hope is the better PROG album. It's a complete start-to-finish concept album, maintaining Its narrative and its particular symphonic, often almost martial style of rock-adjacent music from beginning to end, albeit with discrete pieces that have their own character. The story is a sort of sci-fi epic with plenty of 60's style peace and love vs oppression and repression themes woven in. There's little of the winking tongue-in-cheek feel of the first album; while these lads don't take themselves so seriously that humor is absent from the mix, there's no overt Rugglesby or Anus of Uranus moments here. 1977 was well before "steampunk" was a genre, but the band's musical and narrative approach on Hope isn't a million miles away from fitting the general retro Victorian in space feel. It's a fun and sometimes genuinely emotive ride that I highly recommend to those of us that can still maintain our attention span for an entire LP. A work of masterful but not demonstrative musicianship, as well as a somewhat poignant glimpse of a time when the 1960s spirit was still strong enough to inspire 1970s bands to baroque statements, before the fashionable and generational fault lines banished such wonderfully over-the-top musical statements to the margins.
items._cn_summary: Klaatu乐队1977年发行的专辑《Hope》是一张完整的概念专辑，融合交响乐与摇滚元素，以科幻史诗为叙事框架，融入六十年代反战与和平主题。音乐风格偏向宏大叙事型前卫摇滚，编曲以巴洛克式陈述见长，乐手技艺精湛但内敛克制。整体呈现复古未来主义的维多利亚太空感，兼具军事化节奏与情感张力。作为主流厂牌发行的作品，定位偏传统交响前卫摇滚领域，在实验性与先锋性方面突破有限，更适合钟情于七十年代古典化前卫传统的听众。

items.body:
Tarantino muse, Japanese actress and singer, Meiko Kaji’s 1974 album is given the reissue stardust treatment on its first new edition in 50+ years.

“Wewantsounds is delighted to continue its extensive reissue program of Meiko Kaji's early discography, originally released by Teichiku Records in Japan between 1972 and 1974. The Quentin Tarantino muse—famous for her starring roles in Lady Snowblood and Stray Cat Rock—was also a gifted singer. Otoko Onna Kokoro No Aika is another collection of superb cinematic songs featuring Kaji's signature mix of Japanese Pop and Groove, backed by lush, atmospheric orchestrations. This includes her rendition of "Tokyo Nagare Mono," the theme song for Seijun Suzuki's cult 1966 film Tokyo Drifter. This reissue features the original artwork and a eight-page insert with new liner notes by Hashim Kotaro Bharoocha, who interviewed Meiko Kaji for the occasion.”
items._cn_summary: 这是一张1974年日本女歌手Meiko Kaji的专辑再版，由独立厂牌Wewantsounds发行。音乐风格被描述为日式流行与律动的结合，配以层次丰富、氛围浓郁的管弦乐编曲，具有电影配乐般的画面感。专辑收录了其为1966年 cult 电影《东京流浪汉》演唱的主题曲。Meiko Kaji因出演《修罗雪姬》和《流浪猫之 rock》系列电影而知名，也曾因昆汀·塔伦蒂诺的《杀死比尔》选曲而在西方获得 cult 式关注。从音乐本体来看，这张作品属于带有东瀛色彩的电影流行歌曲，虽然氛围制作有一定质感，但整体仍偏向传统日式流行范畴，与实验、前卫、爵士或电子等领域的距离较远。

items.body: Review by ianjferris@gmail.com — Frankly I just do not know what some people are on about. This album is clearly a fully committed Progressive Rock album by Genesis, just as much as any other Genesis album. However, in the absence of Steve Hackett, it is clear that this collection of shorter progressive rock pieces is different in sound and it was the catalyst which caused ears in previously uninformed quarters, to prick up, those ears being the ones that were more interested in, much more radio friendly, standard pop songs. And therein lies the genius and talent of Genesis. This album sees the band (the three members that were left by then) progressing (well it is prog rock after all...) within that 1978 contemporary rock/pop music environment, using newer instruments (Tony's poly moog for example), eschewing the older ones such as the troublesome mellotron (only utilised here on "Many Too Many") but still retaining that long recognised Genesis sound.The confusion for many back in 1978 was that there were no long extended instrumentals containing half a dozen chord changes and twice as many different time signatures. If Genesis had decided to record and release an album like that back then, it may well have been a great double album for prog rock fans. It would also have made it a very safe album for established Genesis fans. But the band and their management knew that they had to modify what they had been doing. They were trying to remain relevant within a changing music environment. They were also dealing with the fact that Mike Rutherford was not yet as accomplished a player as Steve Hackett was. And they also had to attract a wider record buying audience. All of that is what led to the recording of and release of this album as we heard it then and still hear it today.Notwithstanding the fact that it contains some immediately attractive, so called "throwaway pop" pieces for all ears, there is no doubt that like many Progressive Rock albums before it, "...and then there were three..." does take repeated spins before the listener eventually can fully and completely "get into it". But the reality is that Tony Banks' skillful manipulation of the keys is in there, along with Phil Collins' stellar drumming techniques and Mike Rutherford's guitar and bass style does shine through in many places. This is a very rewarding album when it is played many times. It very much grows on the listener. And that goes for every single song. There isn't a weak track on the album.I have no problem in awarding this album 5 stars simply because it is clear that Genesis have created something that contains the complete essence of Progressive Rock music, while sitting very comfortably within a changed world.
items._cn_summary: 这张1978年的专辑是Genesis在吉他手Steve Hackett离队后的转型之作，风格从早期交响前卫摇滚逐渐向更短小、更具流行色彩的曲目靠拢，但仍保留了Tony Banks的键盘功底和Phil Collins的鼓技。制作上引入了Polymoog等较新的合成器，减少了Mellotron的使用，整体呈现七十年代末主流前卫摇滚向流行摇滚过渡的特征。与该用户偏好的实验前卫、自由爵士、电子声响和暗潮等方向相比，该作品偏向主流厂牌下的商业化制作，创新性有限，跨界融合度不高，在实验性和声音设计层面缺乏突破。

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — I've already posted my review of Flea's Topi O Uomini, which I enjoyed very much, so I was excited to see that the band members had another project by the name of Etna. And even better, it was a jazz fusion record, and I do love me some good Italian fusion. So, going into this, I already had some high expectations, and to be honest, I think they were indeed met. This record has that classic, fast-paced, and energetic sound that I love about jazz fusion, never leading me off an edge and keeping my ears open right up until the end. Sure, maybe not the most original music out there, but some strong tunes nevertheless! The album cover also stood up to the musical performance in terms of quality, displaying a provoking collage of various exploding colors and indistinguishable yet intriguing images. Francesco Pennisi did a great job with the art here. As it turns out, his brother, Carlo, played guitar and mandolin in the record. The other musicians include Antonio Marangolo on keyboards, Elio Volpini on bass, and Agostino Marangolo on drums. The record opens with the shortest song on the album (being only a little under 4 minutes long), but I think it does a great job at representing this quirky and fun music that is present throughout the entire album. It may be a little lacking in energy, however, and is the weakest song on this project. However, the material just gets better from here on out. Pretty much every song here is amazing and incorporates very interesting and well-put-together aspects of the band members' capabilities. It's very reminiscent of Arti E Mestieri, weaving and bending across these jams of intricate arrangements that twist every few seconds while simultaneously expanding into every moment. It feels very powerful the way they have their tight grooves kicking throughout the whole record and songs like South East Wind, Golden Idol (which is also the longest piece on the album), and Sentimental Lewdness. Don't be fooled by all this energy though, as the band knows how to make good use of dynamics and includes laid-back and relaxed bits to refresh the listener in a way, sometimes being things such as ambient improvisation and soundscapes, which I find really interesting. In conclusion, Etna is a lovely little record that fits nicer with the Italian fusion and wider Rock Progressivo Italiano scene. Not an essential per se, but definitely a good second-tier album for fans of that type of stuff or those who are generally just looking for more high energy and exciting music along the same lines as Mahavishnu Orchestra or Jean Luc Ponty (but without the violin, unfortunately). This is, in my eyes, deserving of a very strong 4.25/5.
items._cn_summary: 意大利爵士融合乐队Etna于1975年发行的首张专辑，融合了爵士、放克与摇滚元素，属于意大利前卫摇滚场景中的爵士摇滚分支。专辑以快速节奏、紧凑律动和复杂编曲为特点，吉他、键盘、贝斯与鼓之间的配合展现了乐队成员的技术功底。曲风类似Arti E Mestieri和Mahavishnu Orchestra，在动感段落与放松的氛围即兴之间形成动态对比。整体制作扎实，专辑封面由Francesco Pennisi设计，颇具艺术感。作为该流派的二线作品，对融合乐爱好者有一定参考价值，但在创新性上较为有限，乐评本身也承认其并非最具原创性的作品。

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — Riccardo Zappa's debut album, by the name of Celestion, is another one of the heavily unknown albums I pulled from various conversations with friends and colleagues alike about the more underground artists of Rock Progressivo Italiano. It was much more on the lighter and delicate side of the spectrum, with classical Italian folk music playing a big part in the overall makeup of this project. Overall, it's pretty good, with a little too much meandering here and there, but I can still tolerate it. It seems like it had a few too many upbeat, rocking sections than I would've liked, but it was enjoyable nonetheless. Moving on, when it comes to the other musicians on this project, the personnel includes Vince Tempera on keyboards, Julius Farmer on bass, Ottavio Corbellini on drums, and George Aghedo on percussion. All guitars, vocals, and (from what I can tell) songwriting are done by Ricardo. The music can feel a little dull at points, not bringing much interesting nor original material to the table. Sure, it's good, and there are some cool moments of jazzy prog and jamming going on that (admittedly) sometimes ruin the mood of the softer acoustic sections, but for the most part I would say it's quite forgettable. The production also didn't help, as I didn't enjoy the actual sound of the record. I feel like out of the five songs that only add up to around thirty-four minutes of runtime, the opening composition and longest of the bunch, Frammenti, is the strongest. It does a good job at introducing us to the sound we'll be having for the majority of the album, that being mysterious folk bits, sometimes mixed in with vibrant ambience, and then short bursts of fun rock music sprinkled in every few minutes or so. I feel like what this album does get right, however, is the soothing and dreamy feeling of some of the music here. It can flow into a hazy state for a while and float the listener along, but sometimes it can feel inconsistent, and I feel like this album would've actually been better if it was more acoustic-based instead of exciting, though at times tension-breaking, rock music slips into the cracks. Other than that, the songs can go in one ear and out the other and don't really stick that much. In conclusion, this will be one of the weaker records from the Rock Progressivo Italiano scene in my opinion. Without keeping an interesting sound going, I find it hard to really enjoy this record or give anything above a light 3/5.
items._cn_summary: 这是1977年意大利摇滚进步（Rock Progressivo Italiano）场景下的专辑，融合了古典意大利民谣、轻柔原声段落与短促的摇滚乐段，并夹杂部分爵士化的即兴演奏。整体编曲以民谣氛围为主，键盘、贝斯与鼓的配置较为常规，原声吉他与人声贯穿全作。五首曲目共约三十四分钟，开篇曲《Frammenti》被乐评视为最具代表性的作品，展现了神秘民谣与鲜明氛围交织的基调。专辑在意大利地下进步摇滚圈中属于较为冷门的作品，但乐评指出其在原创性与声音辨识度上略显不足，气氛时有断裂，制作水平亦不够突出，整体呈现出可听但难以留下深刻印象的特质。

items.artist: Dominique Cravic et les Primitifs du futur
items.label: Buda Musique
items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris café, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur. Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.

Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I’m guessing here), and musical saw.

Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)

The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle, just to get the list started.

Ukulele Lady (excerpt)

The liner notes point out that “Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.” Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous “Ukulele Lady” from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie’s 1971 album Hobo’s Lullaby. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.

N'oublie pas Gréco (excerpt)

A more serious item is “N’oublie pas Gréco” (Don’t Forget Gréco”) is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gréco, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like “Fumée aux yeux” (“Smoke Gets in Your Eyes”), “Boude pas” (“Take Five”), and “Prive d’amour” (“As Time Goes By”).

This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, “The young have fire, but we have light.” In its own little corner, Les Crimes du Musette shines bright.

Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review)

Carolina Chocolate Drops - Genuine Negro Jig (Review)

items.label: Mig
items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999 documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm “Mac” Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.

Taped at the height of Dr. John’s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.

A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac’s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.

Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic “Iko, Iko,” a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast “Qualified,” wherein the singer warns, “I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.”

Any Dr. John fan will recognize “I Walk on Guilded Splinters,” a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper’s immersion in “funknology” (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: “Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.”

Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own “Sweet Home New Orleans” and “Goin’ Back to New Orleans,” and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington’s “I'm Gonna Go Fishin’.” Among other gems are Mac’s Top–10 hit “Right Place, Wrong Time,” and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King’s “Big Chief,” another Mardi Gras burner.

Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, “I always play a little bit of everything. I think that’s what music’s about: a little bit of somethin’ old, somethin’ in the middle, somethin’ new, and somethin’ as yet uncreated.”

Dr John's’s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of At the Rockpalast is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, “If you’re gonna get off on somethin’ you don’t need to know nothin’ about it. Music is a universal language.”

Dr. John (Mac Rebennack) - Things Happen That Way (Review)

Lakou Mizik - HaitiNola (Review)

items.body:
Editor's note:

When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago.

 

Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we’d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow— both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both.

One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That’s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched.

The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors

By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house—right in the heart of the “‘hood,” beneath the Midway Airport’s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard.

The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors

We were in a section of town that one man defined as “the forgotten parts.” Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city’s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin’ Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby.

The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors

The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who’d asserted “you’ll really want to hear my story,” was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving.

One elder’s tough facade broke down as she shared how she’d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, “I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I’m sorry.”
But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology— for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made.

The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors

Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global, who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally."

When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It’s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

items.body:
Pianist Kenny Barron (b. 1943) has paid his dues, working in the bands of Yusef Lateef and Dizzy Gillespie as well as a three-year stint in trumpeter Freddie Hubbard 's band. His work as a leader has also soared. His first album under his own name was titled You Had Better Listen (Atlantic, 1967). That title offered good advice. As with most top-tier jazz artists who boast 50-plus-year careers, he has played thousands of concerts, and many of these have surely been recorded, only to be forgotten, the tapes shelved. So Zev Feldman —who so often finds and produces for release lost recordings from jazz giants past and present (saxophonist Joe Henderson , pianists Cecil Taylor , Ahmad Jamal , Mal Waldron and Bill Evans , multiple-reedman Yusef Lateef )—offers up a superb trio outing from Barron: So Many Lovely Things: Live In Brecon . The 2-disc set was recorded in 1995 at the Brecon Jazz Festival in Wales with his then-current trio—Ray Drummond on bass and drummer Bill Riley. The music sparkles for the duration of it 100-plus minutes.  Barron's sound has always had a classy sheen, in the manner of Hank Jones and Tommy Flanagan , or—to bring it up to a current player— Bill Cunliffe . Opening with "Oh, Look At Me Now, a 1940 Frank Sinatra vehicle written by Joe Bushkin, the trio's brio and ebullience is on full display. They sound playful and full of the joy of creation as they stretch out the tune to 11 minutes of 'let's see what happens' charm. This is followed up by trumpeter Freddie Hubbard 's "Up Jumped Spring," which sounds majestic and lighthearted before Barron strides into Thelonious Monk 's "Shuffle Boil. Most of the tunes here are extended pieces, the familiar—Ray Noble's  "The Very Thought of You," "Ask Me Now" (another Monk gem) and "The Surrey With The Fringe On Top"—stretched out while maintaining the threads of their original melodies. This is Barron, 30 years into a stellar career, playing at the top of his considerable power, accompanied by an exceptional trio. Barron's previously mentioned first recording was aptly titled, so is So Many Lovely Things .

CD 1: Oh, Look At Me Now; Up Jumped Spring; Shuffle Boil; Time Was; Silent Rain; Ask Me Now.
CD 2: Nikara's Song; The Surrey with the Fringe on Top; The Very Thought of You; Canadian Sunset.

Personnel: Kenny Barron piano Ray Drummond bass, acoustic Ben Riley drums

items.body:
Accomplished flutist Ali Ryerson is one of the most exciting proponents of the instrument in jazz. Over the course of a long career, both performing and teaching, she has honed a unique style. It is rooted in the Western classical tradition.  Yet it has a boppish and soulful spontaneity.  Her 17th release as a leader, simply titled The Ali Ryerson Quartet, showcases her masterful command of the instrument and signature sound. The energetic "Chuck's Tune" is a perfect introduction to this effervescent album. After the band plays the main theme, each member takes a brief solo, setting the stage for Ryerson's intricately constructed improvisation. The flutist's agile lines flitter through the laid-back cadence, creating an impressionistic melody.  Pianist Larry Ham takes center stage with a bluesy embellishment of the main theme. Bassist Lou Pappas follows with lyricism and elegance.  Drummer Tom Melito 's suave solo is punctuated by brief refrains from his bandmates, resulting in a delightful repartee. This type of camaraderie marks the entire recording, giving it a dynamic structure. For instance, on the energetic "Before Today." Pappas tastefully interprets the main theme and exchanges vibrant phrases with Ryerson before the leader launches into a warm and captivating performance.  Ham's response, as he takes his place in the spotlight, is mellifluous and polished.  Ryerson then leads the ensemble in a lively collective discourse that ushers in the tune's exciting conclusion. Ryerson tackles Brazilian bossa nova with the same sophisticated musicianship as American blues. The infectious groove of "Nada Como Ter Amor" that the side men create buoys Ryerson's resonant flute.  Ryerson's well-structured extemporization, nevertheless, crackles with spontaneity and reserved passion.  Ham adds a touch of romance to the song with his cascading notes, especially as he engages the leader in a graceful duet. The swinging "AliCat Blues," meanwhile, opens with Ham's crisp chords.  The rhythm trio's vamps simmer with soul, perfectly complementing Ryerson's cool, haunting musings. On this captivating set, Ryerson demonstrates her mature creativity and undampened, youthful enthusiasm. Ryerson and her side men craft music that is accessible without being humdrum and stimulating without being self-indulgent. The result is a charming and cohesive work that makes for a satisfying listen and should have a wide appeal.

Personnel: Ali Ryerson flute Larry Ham piano Lou Pappas bass Tom Melito drums

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — No one can achieve perfection, even the greatest geniuses fail at times, and, after releasing threemasterpieces of the concept album genre, both as a solo artist and band member in Pink Floyd, RogerWaters releases "Radio K.A.O.S" in 1987, his first album after permanently departing from PinkFloyd. And just as the Floyd was in an identity crisis, releasing a low quality record in 1987, justafter Roger's release, Waters was having a crisis keeping a coherent and interesting sound together,without the help of David Gilmour or Eric Clapton to add melodic weight to his otherwise dense andcomplex records.Trying to find any positive aspects in the melodic and musical qualify of this record is, to say thevery least, difficult, as the compositions themselves are weak, repetitive, unengaging and overlypolished. Just as prog bands like Yes or Genesis were releasing pop albums, Roger Waters does thesame, but unlike them, his compositions try to dance between this thin ice of operatic, dense andheavy music and the softer radios catchy pop of the 80's, two contradictory and incompatible musicalstyles, trying to (forcefully) mix themselves together, thus, they are unbalanced, furthermore, themusical interpretation, musicianship, vocals and sound effects are poor, the drums specially, feellifeless, uninspired and dull, the rest of the instruments barely stand out, and Roger's vocals aremechanical, robotic and two dimensional. We can also say, the sound effects in the middle of thesongs do not act in the same manner as they did in "The wall" or "The pros and cons of hitchhiking",this time, they're out of place and don't have good timing, eclipsing the actual music.Production wise, the album has mediocre mixing and mastering, the drums being too loud andreverberating, the bass hidden underneath walls of sound, Roger's voice equalized in a way thatmakes the lower pitch parts stand out too much without putting any attention to mid and highpitches, the guitars and synths hidden underneath sound effects and the incredibly loud drums and,to no one's surprise, all of this extremely compressed and claustrophobic, this doesn't help thealready weak compositions, this just creates an exhausting and unappealing, unmelodic, disorientingmess of a record.If I had to say something positive about the record, it's the concept, it follows the story of adisabled man called Billy talking to a DJ through a radio call, telling the story of his life andhow police repression and poverty ruined him, this would be a great critique of inequality andabandonment if it weren't for the unnecessary addition of nuclear war, which doesn't add anything tothe recor (as the threat of nuclear war was thawing at the time) ,except eclipsing the great aspects of the concept, this nuclear premise (which ends the album, since we can interpret that Billy dies in a nuclear attack at the end of the story) is straight up forced, the album would have been much better if it just stayed on the concept of poverty, abandonment and repression.Overall, it's one of the most boring records I've ever listened to, pretentious in a negative way,loud and unlistenable and uninspired. Unless you're a hardcore Roger Waters/Pink Floyd fan, I'd sayskip this record, and go straight to it's follow up album "Amused to death".My dearest of respects to the talented musicians who played on the album, since they were sadly, drowned by poor compositions and production.
items._cn_summary: 罗杰·沃特斯1987年发行的跨界前卫摇滚专辑，作为其永久离开平克·弗洛伊德后的首张个人作品。整张专辑以电台DJ与残疾青年比利通话为叙事框架，试图将叙事性概念融入80年代流行化的摇滚制作中。编曲上以合成器、鼓机和电吉他为主打，融入大量音效和无线电采样元素，呈现出典型的80年代数字制作质感。配器大量依赖鼓机节奏与人声采样，技术手法与同时期主流摇滚唱片厂牌的商业制作一致。概念层面涉及社会不平等与核战争威胁等议题，叙事通过无线电传输这一媒介串联。整体音乐风格偏向主流流行摇滚，与实验、前卫电子、暗潮等流派距离较远，商业化导向明显，在创新性与声音探索方面较为有限。

items.label: Hudson
items.body:
In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter’s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages – and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice.

Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy, with its famous lines:

“Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.”

Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It’s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he’s selected some great talent to help – guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator.

Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid

For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like “Sam Bamford” and “Mary Fildes,” while the three short pieces that comprise “The Monkey Rides The Mare” capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers.

Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid

Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat.

In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It’s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time.

items.label: Nonesuch
items.body:
A little before the end of the last century, a revelatory compilation appeared, seemingly from nowhere. From Where I Stand: The Black Experience In Country Music opened a window on something so many didn’t even know existed to show that country music had never been a white preserve. That album was a few years before the Carolina Chocolate Drops burst on the scene, reclaiming the Black heritage in country and string band music, plus a great deal more. Genuine Negro Jig, their third release, saw them move up to the prestigious Nonesuch label, a powerful artistic imprimatur, winning them a Grammy for an album very far removed from the mainstream.

Genuine Negro Jig (15th Anniversary Edition) by Carolina Chocolate Drops

This expanded 15th anniversary edition marks a good time to look back at the band’s mix of Piedmont string band and traditional music, nestling beside early 20th century blues, and a few original and modern pieces in the mix (like the Tom Waits-penned “Trampled Rose”). The trio roared into the music, playing it with fire and unalloyed joy – yet also with plenty of subtlety; list to “Snowden’s Jig (Genuine Negro Jig)” for a taste of how the members worked together.

For many, this would have been the first opportunity to hear Rhiannon Giddens – quite a big global star these days – and Don Flemons, as well as Sule Greg Wilson, standard bears for an idea whose time had come.

This is an album very much worth of this deluxe reissue treatment, a real landmark, not simply for the career of the Carolina Chocolate Drops, but for roots music in general. And people responded – hence that Grammy.

Genuine Negro Jig (15th Anniversary Edition) by Carolina Chocolate Drops

There are plenty of bonus tracks here, all worth hearing, but the real meat is on the original release. There’s the delicious, sultry blues of “Why Don’t You Do Right?”, the wild string band abandon of “Cindy Gal,” Giddens’s unaccompanied voice on “Reynardine,” and the full-tilt race through “Sandy Boys.” It’s exhilarating, but so much more. There’s deep thought given to the arrangements and the interplay between instruments and voices.

Genuine Negro Jig (15th Anniversary Edition) by Carolina Chocolate Drops

The band aren’t purists. They don’t need to be. Whatever the sources for the material, they transform it and turn it into something that speaks with their voice. Released a decade after From Where I Stand, Genuine Negro Jig was a bold manifesto that still speaks loudly today. It is an album very much worth of this deluxe reissue, waiting for a new audience to discover.

items.body:
The release of Crazy World of Love marks a new chapter for Louise Alexandra, a jazz vocalist whose artistry is as deep as her background is unconventional. Splitting her time between the vanguard of medical science and the timeless traditions of jazz, Alexandra is a Dutch-American vocalist, songwriter, and active cancer research scientist. For over 15 years, she built a formidable reputation within Boston's highly competitive biotech and jazz circuits before returning to the Netherlands, where she continues to develop cancer therapies while pursuing her musical evolution with enhanced focus. Alexandra's former name was Louise van Aarsen (that would be, Dr. Louise van Aarsen) before she sharpened her professional image as a singer. As a scientist, Alexandra concentrates on drug discovery, inflammation, vaccines, immunoassays, and genomics. She has successfully straddled the left-brain and right-brain worlds of science and music. Central to Alexandra's vocal identity is her profound association with the late Rebecca Parris , widely revered as Boston's "First Lady of Jazz" and a peer to legends like Sarah Vaughan and Carmen McRae . As Parris' student and trusted protégé, Alexandra absorbed the master's lessons in emotional delivery, phrasing, and stagecraft. Parris didn't just teach Alexandra; she actively mentored her career, directing and shaping her earliest recorded statements. Crazy World of Love stands on the shoulders of two previous, critically-respected studio albums that highlight Alexandra's steady artistic trajectory: the Parris-directed Destiny (Self Produced, 2012), recorded with premier Boston jazz musicians, established her clean, traditional sensibilities and sophisticated tone grownup music for grownups. Also directed by Parris was the follow-up recording, Today (Self Produced, 2020). This release revealed an increased confidence, deeper emotional nuance, and an expanding repertoire. While her previous catalog firmly rooted her in the rich tradition of the New England jazz scene, Crazy World of Love represents a major geographical and stylistic leap. Collaborating with Dutch jazz royalty—including pianist Rob van Bavel and his trio—Alexandra steps fully into her own as a lyricist and arranger, seamlessly bridging her American jazz upbringing with a vibrant European sensibility. The recording has several highlights, including Emmett Cohen Trio 's "Angel of Mine," to which Alexandra penned lyrics she shared with Benny Bernack III , who also played flugelhorn on the song. The singer breaks out her impressive vocalese chops on "East of the Sun," "Crazy World of Love," and "Hershey Bar / Little Did I Dream." The singer gets personal on the ballad "We Had It All." Alexandra paints a very adult picture of growing together and apart sans any romantic affect. She tells it like it is. The spirit of Parris, always close, becomes tactile on the "Some Other Time / We'll Be Together Again" diptych. Alexandra creates a panorama of love in all its guises on Crazy World of Love .

Personnel: Louise Alexandra vocals Rob van Bavel piano Frans van Geest bass, acoustic Marcel Serierse drums Vincent Koning guitar Jan Menu saxophone Benny Benack III trumpet and vocals

items.body: Review by TenYearsAfter — For the first time in many, many years I gave this album a try (I got rid off it after two listening sessions when it was released in 1978), unfortunately it still doesn't appeal to me. There are obvious hints from the previous albums Wind & Wuthering and A Trick Of The Tail, music that carries me away, but on ATTWT I can appreciate only a few good compositions but mostly my prog pleasure is brutally interrupted by songs that are more melodic rock and even pop (like the awful Follow You Follow Me). What I miss is the wonderful interaction between Banks and Hackett (trademark 70-77 Genesis), they inspired each other to an extreme level. After Hackett left Genesis he found a kind of new Tony Banks in Nick Magnus, I embraced Hackett solo and said goodbey to the Genesis trio. Simply because for me they had turned into another band, hardly the captivating symphonic rock as on their previous efforts.My rating 2,5 star.

items.body: As an ardent admirer of Petrenko’s Liverpool Shostakovich cycle (Naxos), I was excited to hear his first Mahler recording for Harmonia Mundi — and it does not disappoint. Symphony No. 3 Amazon Presto Apple In recent years I have reviewed two other performances of this work: the Czech PO under Bychkov (Pentatone – review) and the Minnesota SO under Vänskä (BIS – review). Both feature gorgeous orchestral sound that disguises lackluster interpretations. Both labels provide a deep and wide soundstage, with the largest possible dynamic range in a complementary acoustic that adds a certain homogenous glow to the strings. By comparison, Harmonia Mundi’s live recording, made in the Royal Albert Hall, London, on 27 April 2023, is closely miked, and occasionally sounds constricted: there is an occasional balance issue, and little bloom around the sound. But on repeated hearing the ear adjusts, giving us an opportunity to hear this orchestra playing at the top of its considerable game. Petrenko shapes the first movement with a sure hand, never letting it feel like a series of disjointed episodes. Mahler described this music as “hardly anything but sounds of nature,” a description that surely requires the hyper-expressive performance heard here. The opening implacable horn pronouncement leads to brooding, elemental urgings from the lower instruments; Matthew Gee’s wonderful trombone solo ensures the struggle for life is very much heard and felt. I admire the willingness of the woodwinds to make beauty of execution secondary to vivid characterization: just listen to those squawking piccolos and shrieking E-flat clarinets. Many performances downplay the moments where Mahler asks for different tempos at the same time, but Petrenko and his players positively revel in it (sample the solo violin and horn around 18’20”); the ‘Rabble’ music (right around 21’50”) is truly disorderly. The frenetic Coda marks the end of one of the most exciting readings in recent years. The first movement’s wildness is countered by a second movement of sweet gentleness, played by the Royal Philharmonic with beauty and nuance. The Scherzo (which quotes from Mahler’s early song Ablösung im Sommer / Relief in Summer) is also successful, though I wanted the offstage posthorn (gorgeously played by Toby Street) to be more distant. Is this the conductor’s choice or an engineering issue? Close miking also negates the sense of delicate shimmering in the string accompaniment. The final terror-filled build-up leads to a driven, frenzied climax. Vasily Petrenko. Photo © Bård Gundersen. The two vocal movements are less impressive. Hanna Hipp’s wide vibrato quickly develops a pronounced beat, and she seems unwilling to sing softly. Her generalized somber interpretation is no match for the sensitive expressiveness of Janet Baker (LSO/Tilson Thomas/Sony Classical), Christa Ludwig (NYPO Bernstein/DG), and Birgit Remmert (CBSO/Rattle/Warner Classics). The fifth movement is lustily dispatched (with fabulous orchestral bells), though the joyful excellence of the Tiffin Boys’ Choir is somewhat hampered by the prominent vibrato from the women of the Philharmonia Chorus. And surely with the mics so close, diction should be more emphatic. The final movement’s tempo marking (Langsam, Slow) is rather generic, allowing for a wide variety of timings: Iván Fischer (BFO/Channel) takes 21’31” whereas Tilson Thomas’s second reading (SFSO) takes 26’31”, more than a minute and a half slower than Bernstein’s second New York Philharmonic reading (DG). I find Abbado’s Berlin performance (22’25”, also recorded live in the Royal Festival Hall in 1999) profoundly moving, but Petrenko, taking about a minute longer, runs a close second, with particularly lovely playing from the strings and principal woodwinds. Towards the end of the Noch etwas bewegter (9’20”), a greater accelerando may have caught more of the pained intensity Abbado and Bernstein find. But Petrenko is careful to keep the brass as delicate coloring through most of the movement, so that when they finally are unleashed in the Coda the sound gains a new powerful radiance that is deeply moving. Bruno Walter described this movement as “a single sound of heartfelt and exalted feelings, in which the whole giant structure finds its culmination.” Certainly, that is true here. Harmonia Mundi’s booklet includes a written introduction by the conductor, fine notes by Dr. Genevieve Robyn Arkle, texts, and translations, as well as the rosters of the orchestra and choirs. I do hope that Petrenko and Harmonia Mundi plan on more Mahler releases (there has been positive press for recent performances of the first and eighth symphonies) — warmly recommended. Posthumous reminder of MF Doom’s landmark classic, following the late, great MC’s death at the end of 2020 - with 11 tracks of bonus material.

A staple of our listening diet upon release in 2004 (probably preceded or followed by a listen to his ‘Special Blends volumes), ‘MM….Food’ still stands up among the greatest and most coveted hip hop albums of our time. Beats to bars, it’s a peerless example of Daniel Dumile Thompson’s MF Doom alias, playing out as a sort of stoned comic book fantasy voiced by a cartoon supervillain, literally inspired by Marvel Comics’ Doctor Doom, whose moniker sounds a bit like MF’s real middle name.  

The album oscillate between Doom’s mind-boggling metaphoric wordplay and his signature instrumentals, adapting the golden era ‘90s style of sampledelic collage and rugged rhymes to his singular purpose, and making a marked step on from his earlier work as Zev Love X with the legendary KMD. By choice or osmosis there’s probably a whole generation of headz who’ve committed the bars of ‘MM….Food’ to memory, and we can only recommend a refresher session right here if you’re rusty. Packing bags of nostalgia and vibes for days, it’s a true evergreen.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自美国肯塔基州小镇奥尔巴尼的艺术家Colton Bowlin，发表于《Songlines》杂志。肯塔基州地处阿巴拉契亚地区，该地区以美国传统民间音乐、乡村蓝草和原声民谣风格著称。从现有信息来看，这很可能是一张以美国南方民间/根源音乐为底色的作品，融合了地方口述传统与乡村器乐元素。乐评内容严重不足，仅有开篇寥寥数语便被截断，无法了解其具体的音乐编排、制作手法或艺术立场。就用户偏好而言，美国传统民间音乐属于常规民谣范畴，与实验、前卫、自由爵士、电子或暗潮等方向距离较远，缺乏明显的跨界实验信号。整体定位偏向区域性本土创作，特色有限。

items._cn_summary: Geary & John 是一支以原声吉他二重奏形式呈现的蓝草音乐组合，首支单曲采用1951年古董Martin吉他一次性录制完成，不做任何叠录。歌曲主题围绕一个缺乏动力却以轻松态度看待生活的男性展开，带有幽默色彩。整体而言，这是一首传统美国蓝草风格的民谣作品，蓝草作为纯民谣类别与用户偏好的实验、前卫、爵士、电子等方向距离较远。文章本身内容较短，更接近新闻通稿而非深度乐评，信息量有限，难以对音乐的艺术价值做出充分评估。

items.body:
Well, they almost did it. The duo known as Crown Lands made an album that just about meets the hype it has received. Most people were sour on the two EPs they delivered after 2023’s acclaimed Fearless. I understand: Those works, the semi-ambient, semi-world music instrumental Ritual I and Ritual II, arguably weren’t particularly ambitious and they certainly strayed from Fearless. But I enjoyed them. With Apocalypse, they are largely back to the formula that so many loved on Fearless: Several short or mid-length tunes, along with an epic.

There are two notable differences between the albums, one objective and one subjective to my ears. First, the objective: Apocalypse is 15 minutes shorter, clocking in at a concise 42 minutes. Second, the subjective: I don’t think Apocalypse is as traditionally “progressive” as Fearless. Rather, I view it as a bold and sometimes challenging hard-rock album that more resembles Led Zeppelin than Rush. I mean that not just in the vocals, which this time around sound more like Robert Plant than Geddy Lee, but also in the arrangements. We’re even given a couple tunes that recall hair metal in “Blackstar” and “The Fall,” the latter featuring some disco elements. The low point is "The Revenants I", a ballad that has been a consistent skip for me. Thankfully, it is followed by the majestic closer. At 19 minutes, the title track gives a Crown Lands fan pretty much all that they may want.

This album is excellent at times, but sags somewhat in the middle with tracks four, five, and especially six. So, I can’t quite give it 4.5 stars but, instead, 4 very strong stars.
items._cn_summary: 加拿大二人组Crown Lands的专辑《Apocalypse》以硬摇滚为核心框架，编曲明显受到Led Zeppelin及Hair Metal影响，嗓音风格接近Robert Plant。专辑时长四十二分钟，末尾的十九分钟同名曲是目前作品中最具前卫摇滚色彩的段落。少量曲目融入迪斯科元素，乐评指出部分歌曲偏主流硬摇套路。此前发表的Ritual I与II曾尝试氛围音乐与世界音乐方向，但本作基本回归硬摇滚路线。整体结构为多首短曲加一首长篇史诗。该作品在硬摇滚框架内制作扎实，但与实验音乐、前卫爵士、电子、世界融合等方向交集有限。
